text:
The question is whether P9's compatibility objection requires any change to an account of global availability, and if so what P7's target distinction identifies as being questioned. The frozen material supplies P7 on criticism targets, P9 on local alternatives and global bounds with the correlation loss objection, and a prior E009 criticism whose standing is explicitly unendorsed, concerning a Lean expression rather than P7 or P9 themselves. Nothing in the packet asserts that the missing constraint exists. I will build a small construction that connects the two, mark exactly which parts are the source's and which are mine, and name the observation or interpretation that would matter.

What P9 supplies, taken at face value, is: per-booking reservations are quantities of greatest-revision active holds, or zero, or unresolved among tied greatest-revision active holds; global availability is capacity minus the sum; the sum is not well-defined when there are unresolved alternatives; per-booking minimum and maximum give a global interval; intervals lose correlations because a booking-A high alternative may be incompatible with a booking-B high alternative if they share an unnamed physical resource; the snapshot does not name physical resources, so this incompatibility is invisible; a conjecture is that the snapshot is under-specified for any real warehouse; a criticism is that exposing alternatives without a resolution policy pushes the problem downstream.

What P7 supplies, taken at face value, is: criticism targets can be a reconstruction rule, a particular record, a booking's history, the snapshot as a whole, or the assumption that logical time is meaningful; "this snapshot is inconsistent" can mean at least three different things (two active greatest-revision holds for one booking; total reservations exceeding capacity; logical time behind an expected expiry); a conjecture that many apparent availability disagreements are disagreements about targets; a criticism of the supersession rule differs from a criticism of a high-revision implausible-quantity record; preserving the distinction matters because one can reject a rule while accepting data, or accept a rule while rejecting data.

I will not restate these. The construction below adds an organization that neither passage contains by itself.

## 1. The distinction I add: bound-arithmetic target vs bound-correspondence target

P9 treats the correlation objection as if it bears on the availability calculation. Read literally, the sentence "intervals lose correlations" points at the interval representation, i.e., at the pair (lower bound, upper bound) of the availability number. But the sentence continues: the incompatibility is "invisible" because the snapshot does not name physical resources. That continuation names a missing constraint, not a numerical error. The two halves of P9's objection are therefore already doing different work, but P9 does not separate them and P7 does not name them.

I propose that the correlation objection actually splits P7's "snapshot-as-a-whole" target into two further targets:

- **Bound-arithmetic target.** The claim that the reported interval [capacity minus sum of per-booking maxima, capacity minus sum of per-booking minima] is the correct availability interval for this snapshot. This target is a claim about arithmetic given per-booking possibility sets.
- **Bound-correspondence target.** The claim that the reported interval corresponds to the set of actually realizable global configurations. This target is a claim about the relation between the snapshot's data and an unstated availability-relevant structure.

Under this split, the correlation objection is not a criticism of the availability account's arithmetic. The arithmetic can be correct — capacity minus maxima is indeed a lower bound over the product of per-booking possibility sets — while the correspondence claim fails whenever the product set is not the realizable set. Booking A's high alternative can co-occur with booking B's high alternative in the product set and not co-occur in the warehouse. So the interval can be arithmetically right and correspondentially wrong. P7's distinction between "criticizing a rule" and "criticizing data" does not by itself name this split, because both halves of the correlation objection target the snapshot as a whole rather than any rule or record. The additional distinction is between two sub-targets of the same snapshot-level claim, distinguished by whether the claim is internal to the arithmetic or external to the modeled structure.

This distinction is mine. Nothing in P7 or P9 says that "snapshot-as-a-whole" contains these two sub-targets. P9's own sentence "intervals lose correlations" would, read alone, suggest the objection is about intervals; my reading redirects it to a gap between modeled and realizable joint configurations.

## 2. Why the compatibility objection does not force a change to the arithmetic account

P9's own framing makes the compatibility a conditional: "might be incompatible." The physical resource is "not named in the snapshot." Given those two facts, the claim "the interval is the best available bound" is not refuted. The claim "the interval corresponds to what can actually happen" is refuted only under the additional premise that a resource constraint exists that the snapshot does not record. Neither premise is in the packet.

So my proposed account is:

- No change is required to the availability arithmetic if "availability" is read as the interval over the product of per-booking possibility sets. That interval is a well-defined, arithmetically correct summary of the snapshot's per-booking alternatives.
- A change is required to any claim that this interval characterizes what the warehouse can actually do. If the pre-theoretic question is "how much can be promised without violating capacity," and if capacity is only one of several shared constraints, then the interval is a projection of a set the snapshot does not determine.

This is not a new language component. It is a re-description of what "availability" is a name for: the bound on a modeled product set, not the bound on a physical possibility set. The distinction between the two names is what the correlation objection actually forces. P9 slips between them ("availability is then capacity minus whatever reservation is actually selected" earlier, "interval" later), and P7's "snapshot-as-a-whole" target is not fine-grained enough to catch the slip.

I am not installing a repair. I am proposing that the correlation objection is best classified, in P7's sense, as a criticism of the snapshot-as-a-whole that specifically fails the correspondence half and leaves the arithmetic half alone. If this is right, then the E009 criticism's preoccupation with whether WHL's `availability_lower_bound` and `availability_upper_bound` are named backwards is addressing the arithmetic half, not the correspondence half. P9's correlation objection would survive any repair of those names.

## 3. Criticism of the proposal

**Objection 1 — Is the split real or verbal?** One could say the arithmetic claim just is the correspondence claim under a different description, since "capacity minus maxima" is only meaningful as a bound on a set. Reply: the two come apart when the per-booking possibility sets are not the projections of any joint possibility set. Then "capacity minus maxima" is a well-defined number describable without reference to any joint set, and it can be reported even when no joint set exists. That is exactly the case P9 describes.

**Objection 2 — Does the split do new work, or just rename?** It changes what a reader should look at. Under P9's framing as written, a reader who rejects the interval is invited to look at the interval machinery. Under my split, a reader who rejects the interval may need to look at whether the snapshot is being asked a question it cannot answer. The E009 criticism's repairs to WHL's naming do not address the latter. That is new work.

**Objection 3 — Is calling this a "target" rather than a "reading" consistent with P7?** P7 names snapshot-as-a-whole as a target; my split subdivides that target rather than introducing a new kind of object. If someone thinks P7's list of targets is exhaustive and indivisible, the split is a disagreement with P7's taxonomy, not with P9's objection. I flag this rather than resolve it.

**Objection 4 — Doesn't the correspondence failure only matter if you care about physical realizability?** Yes. The split only matters for a reader whose question is about the warehouse rather than about the snapshot. P9 itself does not stipulate that question. The criticism's scope is narrower than P9's phrasing suggests. This is a partial defense of the original framing.

## 4. What observation or interpretation would matter

The split is decided by whether one can exhibit a snapshot and an unstated resource model where the per-booking possibility sets have a product set strictly larger than the realizable set. P9's example (bookings A and B with high alternatives sharing an unnamed resource) is an illustration, not a case. A demonstration would require: a named resource not modeled by capacity, per-booking possibility sets from the snapshot, and at least one joint configuration in the product set that violates the resource. Without such a demonstration, the split is a distinction in search of a case.

Alternatively, the split fails if "availability" is stipulated to range only over the modeled product set. Then no correspondence claim is being made, and P9's phrasing "intervals lose correlations" is simply an admission about the interval representation rather than a criticism of a further claim. Under that stipulation, my split collapses back into the arithmetic half.

So the discriminating interpretation is: does any account of "availability" for this snapshot implicitly claim correspondence with a realizable joint set, or is the name reserved for a summary over the product set? P7 does not decide this; P9 does not decide it. The packet supplies the demand for the distinction, not its resolution.

## 5. Relationship of the E009 criticism to this construction

The E009 criticism is explicitly unendorsed. Its main targets (WHL's naming backwards for availability bounds, `expired_deletes_rule` not actually deleting, `Commitment := Prop` losing account-relativity, revision having no totality) are about the Lean layer's internal coherence and about whether WHL can express P7's target list. Under my split, those are defects of the arithmetic-side formalization and of the target-list formalization. They do not engage P9's correspondence-side objection, because WHL has no primitive for joint realizability beyond the capacity sum. The E009 criticism actually notes this: "intervals lose correlations… WHL cannot represent non-convex sets or correlations across bookings… Proposed repair: add a resource model or a possible-worlds set. Not installed." That proposed repair names the correspondence side, but E009 treats it as one item in a list rather than as the item that survives every repair of the arithmetic side. My construction moves it to the front and says which half of P9 it belongs to.
